request.system:
You explain a fitted credit-risk model to a credit risk manager who is not a data scientist. You receive the facts about one model and write a short explanation of what drives its predictions of default.

# The text

- Write 5 to 8 sentences in plain English, most important drivers first.
- Mention an interaction when it matters for the model's predictions.
- Say only what the facts support. Do not round a weak effect up to a strong one, and do not add knowledge about credit risk that the facts do not show.
- When the facts do not settle something, say so ("the data do not settle whether ...") or leave it out.

# The answer

Return one JSON object with one list, `sentences`, each with an `id` (1, 2, 3, ...) and its `text`.
messages:
These are the facts about the model.

Model: an explainable boosting machine (EBM), fitted to predict whether a credit applicant defaults (30,000 applicants). Effects are on the log-odds scale: positive values raise the risk of default. Every band is a 95% band from 100 refits of the model on resampled data.

Features, in the order of their share of the model's importance:
- `PAY_0`: repayment status in September 2005, the latest month (-1 paid in full, 1 to 9 months of payment delay; -2 and 0 are not in the data dictionary, commonly read as no consumption and revolving credit used).
  Share of importance 37.7% (95% band 34.6% to 41.2%); rank 1 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= -1: -0.2; 0: -0.6; 1: +0.7; >= 2: +2.4 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +2.52, 95% band [+2.39, +2.64]).
- `LIMIT_BAL`: amount of the given credit in NT dollars, individual and family (supplementary) credit.
  Share of importance 19.6% (95% band 17.5% to 22.0%); rank 2 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 74999: +0.48; 75000-164999: +0.007; >= 165000: -0.3 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -1.06, 95% band [-1.26, -0.92]).
- `PAY_AMT1`: amount paid in September 2005, the latest month, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 11.9% (95% band 9.1% to 13.7%); rank 3 to 4 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 1999: +0.2; 2000-6222: -0.09; >= 6223: -0.4 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -0.67, 95% band [-0.83, -0.50]).
- `BILL_AMT1`: amount of the bill statement in September 2005, the latest month, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 8.8% (95% band 5.2% to 10.8%); rank 3 to 6 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 9000: -0.18; 9001-167251: +0.063; >= 167252: +0.4 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.71, 95% band [+0.37, +0.86]).
- `PAY_AMT2`: amount paid in August 2005, the month before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 5.2% (95% band 3.1% to 8.4%); rank 4 to 7 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): falls by 0.21 (95% band [-0.46, -0.10]) from x = 0 (5th percentile) to x = 19,000 (95th percentile); the shape in between is not resolved at this sample size.
- `AGE`: age in years.
  Share of importance 3.5% (95% band 2.3% to 5.5%); rank 5 to 8 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): rises by 0.30 (95% band [+0.12, +0.44]) from x = 23 (5th percentile) to x = 53 (95th percentile); the shape in between is not resolved at this sample size.
- `BILL_AMT2`: amount of the bill statement in August 2005, the month before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 3.4% (95% band 1.1% to 6.7%); rank 4 to 8 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): rises by 0.21 (95% band [+0.05, +0.41]) from x = 0 (5th percentile) to x = 195,000 (95th percentile); the shape in between is not resolved at this sample size.
- `EDUCATION`: education (1 graduate school, 2 university, 3 high school, 4 others; 0, 5 and 6 are not in the data dictionary).
  Share of importance 2.5% (95% band 0.7% to 3.3%); rank 6 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): rises by 0.15 (95% band [+0.04, +0.20]) from x = 1 (5th percentile) to x = 3 (95th percentile); the shape in between is not resolved at this sample size.
- `PAY_AMT3`: amount paid in July 2005, two months before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 0.1% (95% band 0.2% to 2.2%); rank 8 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -0.00, 95% band [-0.09, +0.13]).

Interactions: the model has 5 pairs. The larger ones:
- `BILL_AMT1 & AGE`: share of importance 2.7% (95% band 1.5% to 3.1%).
  Effect of `BILL_AMT1` from 0 to 201,000: +0.97 (95% band +0.59 to +1.13) when `AGE` = 23, +0.35 (95% band +0.08 to +0.58) when `AGE` = 53.
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.50 (95% band +0.28 to +0.63) when `BILL_AMT1` = 0, -0.12 (95% band -0.31 to +0.15) when `BILL_AMT1` = 201,000.
- `AGE & BILL_AMT2`: share of importance 2.0% (95% band 1.2% to 2.3%).
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.38 (95% band +0.18 to +0.56) when `BILL_AMT2` = 0, -0.03 (95% band -0.20 to +0.24) when `BILL_AMT2` = 195,000.
  Effect of `BILL_AMT2` from 0 to 195,000: +0.40 (95% band +0.17 to +0.58) when `AGE` = 23, -0.01 (95% band -0.19 to +0.26) when `AGE` = 53.
- `PAY_AMT1 & BILL_AMT2`: share of importance 0.9% (95% band 0.0% to 1.2%).
  Effect of `PAY_AMT1` from 0 to 18,400: -0.57 (95% band -0.91 to -0.21) when `BILL_AMT2` = 0, -0.95 (95% band -1.10 to -0.50) when `BILL_AMT2` = 195,000.
  Effect of `BILL_AMT2` from 0 to 195,000: +0.46 (95% band +0.05 to +0.63) when `PAY_AMT1` = 0, +0.08 (95% band -0.21 to +0.47) when `PAY_AMT1` = 18,400.
- `PAY_AMT1 & AGE`: share of importance 0.8% (95% band 0.0% to 1.3%).
  Effect of `PAY_AMT1` from 0 to 18,400: -0.63 (95% band -0.81 to -0.44) when `AGE` = 23, -0.79 (95% band -0.94 to -0.52) when `AGE` = 53.
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.37 (95% band +0.13 to +0.51) when `PAY_AMT1` = 0, +0.20 (95% band +0.04 to +0.45) when `PAY_AMT1` = 18,400.
- `PAY_0 & EDUCATION`: share of importance 0.8% (95% band 0.0% to 1.2%).
  Effect of `PAY_0` from -2 to 2: +2.47 (95% band +2.38 to +2.63) when `EDUCATION` = 1, +2.64 (95% band +2.39 to +2.76) when `EDUCATION` = 3.
  Effect of `EDUCATION` from 1 to 3: +0.13 (95% band +0.03 to +0.20) when `PAY_0` = -2, +0.30 (95% band +0.04 to +0.34) when `PAY_0` = 2.

Write the explanation.

content.text: {"sentences":[{"id":1,"text":"The model's predictions of default are driven mostly by how the applicant has been paying recently: the repayment status in September 2005 accounts for about 38% of the model's importance, and a payment delay of two or more months adds a large amount to the predicted risk of default, while being paid in full lowers it."},{"id":2,"text":"The size of the credit limit is the second most important factor, at about 20% of importance: small limits (under about 75,000 NT dollars) push predicted risk up, while large limits (165,000 NT dollars or more) push it down, with the total swing across typical applicants being moderate in size."},{"id":3,"text":"The amount paid in September 2005 is the third most important factor, at about 12%: larger payments are associated with lower predicted risk, with payments of 6,223 NT dollars or more lowering it noticeably."},{"id":4,"text":"The September 2005 bill amount matters less, at about 9%: high bills (167,252 NT dollars or more) raise predicted risk, and the importance of this feature is uncertain, with its share ranging from about 5% to 11%."},{"id":5,"text":"Age, education, and the August 2005 payment and bill amounts each contribute only a few percent of importance, and their effects are modest; the July 2005 payment amount shows no effect that the data can distinguish from zero."},{"id":6,"text":"The model contains a few interactions that change how strongly some factors matter: for example, the effect of a large September bill is much stronger for younger applicants than for older ones, and the effect of a higher September payment is weaker for older applicants."},{"id":7,"text":"The data do not settle the exact meaning of two repayment-status codes (-2 and 0) that are not in the data dictionary, so how the model treats those applicants is uncertain."}]}
